title: Names and Faces
tagline: A Roman envoy who learned every senator's name in one day, and a method for the thing most people say they are worst at.
card: How to keep a name after you hear it once: pick a feature, turn the name into a picture, and join the two.
goal: you will learn a five-step method for names and faces: hear and repeat, pick a feature, turn the name into a picture, link them, and review.

left_off.q: Why is it a good idea to choose the system to suit the job?
left_off.a: A small number needs a quick tool; a long number needs a bigger one. Using the biggest tool for a small task wastes time.

left_off.q: How many digits does a PAO scene hold, and how many does a Dominic scene hold?
Why did we call Haraguchi's result 'reported'?
left_off.a: The recital was widely reported but not officially certified.

text: Rome, a little over two thousand years ago. A foreign ambassador, Cineas, arrives from the court of King Pyrrhus of Epirus, who is at war with Rome and wants to talk. He has a problem that anyone who has been to a big party will recognise. The Senate has hundreds of members. Everyone expects to be greeted by name. And the ambassador has never met any of them.

The Roman writer Pliny the Elder, who collected examples of great memories in his Natural History, says that Cineas managed it. On the day after he arrived in Rome, he greeted all the senators, and all the knights, by name.

check.a: According to Pliny, he learned the names of all the senators and knights in Rome the day after arriving.

parts.talk: How do you feel when someone you have just met uses your name correctly? And when they forget it?

text: Pliny gives other examples. He says King Cyrus could call every soldier in his army by name. He says a Roman, Lucius Scipio, knew the names of all the citizens of Rome. He says King Mithridates, who ruled twenty-two peoples, could give judgments in each of their languages. Whether every detail is true, the stories show what people admired: a leader who knew your name.
A name is the most personal word there is. To remember it is a way of saying you matter to me. And to forget it, people tell us, is one of the most painful social mistakes.

check.q: Why do you think leaders in the old stories remembered names?
check.a: Knowing a person's name shows respect and builds loyalty. A name is the most personal word.

parts.talk: Tell about a time someone remembered your name when you did not expect it. How did it feel?

text: Why do we forget names so easily? Because when we are introduced, we are usually busy thinking about what to say, or how we look. The name comes in at one ear and goes out at the other. It is also an abstract word: Greg is not a picture, and a face with a new name on it is a bundle of unconnected facts.
The cure is to turn the name into a picture, and fasten that picture to something you notice in the face. It takes about five seconds, and it works because a name is no longer a sound but a scene.

check.q: Why do we forget names so easily?
check.a: We do not pay attention when introduced, and a name is an abstract word with nothing to hold it to the face.

parts.talk: What do you usually do in the first few seconds after someone tells you their name?

words.m: a person sent to speak for a ruler or country. An envoy to Rome.
a noticeable part of a face. Her main feature was her red hair.
easy to see; standing out. A prominent chin.
an idea or word you cannot see or touch.
to fix one thing to another.
the moment when you meet someone and say your names.

source: Pliny the Elder, Natural History VII, lists these feats of memory (Cyrus, Lucius Scipio, Cineas, Mithridates). Retold here in our own words.

method.x: A name is a sound; a face is a picture. The method joins them in a scene.

items.x: Slow down. Look at the person, and ask them to repeat the name or spell it if you are not sure.
Use it at once: 'Nice to meet you, Greg.' Then once or twice more in the conversation.
Pick something about the face or hair that you notice first: ears, eyebrows, a smile, glasses. Pick a feature, not a judgement.

items.h: Turn the name into a picture.
items.x: A sound-alike or a meaning: Greg = a gremlin, Rose = a rose, Carmen = a car full of men.
Make the picture act on the feature, and exaggerate: a gremlin is swinging from Greg's huge ears.

method.title: Greg and his ears
method.given: You meet Greg, who has very large ears.
lines: A gremlin is swinging on each of Greg's huge ears like a child on a swing, shrieking with laughter.
method.pic: A gremlin is swinging from each of Greg's enormous ears.

head: Name
Idea
Picture
rows: a red rose in the hair

items: Pick a feature you could praise: the colour of the eyes, the wave of the hair, the shape of a smile.
Keep your pictures private: they are for your memory, not for saying.
Do not choose features that make you judge the person. A neutral thing, like glasses or hair, is enough.

method.x:
hear it, say it,
find a feature,
picture the name,
join them.

That evening, run through the faces you met, one by one, and say the name picture for each. A name you review the same day will usually stay for a week. Review it again after a few days and you will probably have it for good. You can also place the pictures at places in a palace if you must keep a large number.
Introduce yourself aloud to an imaginary stranger, then 'meet' Greg, Rose and Carmen and say your pictures.

try.title: Greg
try.prompt: Greg is very tall and has curly red hair. Make a scene that joins the name to the feature.
try.model: Greg sounds like gremlin. A gremlin is perched on top of Greg's tall head, twisting his red curls into a nest and singing.
checks: The picture acts on the feature.

try.title: Rose and Carmen
try.prompt: Rose wears round glasses with thick red frames. Carmen has a long, pointed chin. Make a scene for each.
try.model: Rose: red roses grow out of the frames of her glasses, with petals dropping into her coffee. Carmen: a tiny car packed with men drives up and down her long chin, tooting.
checks: Each picture joins to the feature.
The two scenes are very different.

try.title: Victor and Helen
try.prompt: Victor has a gap between his front teeth. Helen has deep dimples. Make a scene for each.
try.model: Victor: a golden cup of victory is balanced in the gap between his front teeth, glowing like a trophy. Helen: a hen is nesting in each of her dimples, clucking.
checks: Each picture is joined to its feature.

try.title: Name to picture
try.prompt: Match the name to the picture that would help you remember it.

items.s: First, hear the name and ___ it at once in conversation.
Then find one ___ of the face, such as the ears or hair.
Finally, join the name picture to the feature in a ___ scene.

try.q: Which feature is the best choice?
opts: Something you could praise, like a bright smile
Something that makes you laugh at their face
try.why: A neutral or admirable feature is kind, and a clear one is easy to find again.

try.title: A first meeting
try.prompt: Pretend you meet a person called Carmen with a pointed chin. Say the name aloud three times in a short conversation, and say your picture.

cards: Hear it: slow down and ask them to repeat if you are not sure.
Say it: use the name at once and twice more.
Find one feature: hair, eyes, ears, smile. A neutral or kind choice.
Turn the name into a picture: sound-alike or meaning.
Join them: the picture acts on the feature, big and moving.
Run through the faces that evening and again after a few days.

quiz.q: Why is a name hard to remember?
opts: It is a sound with no picture and no link to the face
quiz.why: A name has no picture or link, so we let it go.

opts: A word that sounds like another word
A name with the same meaning
A person who looks the same

quiz.q: When should you first review a new name?
quiz.why: Same-day review keeps a name from fading.

quiz.q: What should your private picture be?
quiz.why: The pictures are for your own memory only.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: six new faces
challenge.intro: Six people you have just met. For each, make a name picture and join it to the feature. When the time is up, type the six names, in any order.
challenge.study: One scene per person: name picture + feature.

look_back.q: Which system holds the most digits in one picture?
Name the three parts of a PAO scene.
How does a story chain help you remember a sequence?
look_back.a: Each item leads to the next in a story, so recalling one brings the next.

look_back.q: Why should a picture be unusual?
look_back.a: Ordinary things do not surprise us, so we forget them. Strange, funny or huge pictures stay.

can_do: follow the five steps for a name.
turn a name into a sound-alike or meaning picture.
reflect: Whose name do you most want to remember this week? What is the picture, and where in their face does it sit?
